title: Commonly confused words
lede: The pairs that make smart people look careless in emails, contracts and résumés, with a memory trick for each.

sections.md:
## Why these matter
Spell-check won't catch them: every one is a real word. Readers judge you on them anyway. One *loose* for *lose* in a cover letter can cost an interview. These are the pairs that show up most in professional writing.

## The everyday pairs
| Pair | Use | Trick |
|---|---|---|
| **then / than** | *then* = time; *than* = comparison | th**e**n = wh**e**n; th**a**n = comp**a**re |
| **lose / loose** | *lose* = misplace or fail to win; *loose* = not tight | *loose* has a loose extra *o* |
| **accept / except** | *accept* = receive; *except* = excluding | **ex**cept = **ex**clude |
| **affect / effect** | *affect* = verb (to influence); *effect* = noun (the result) | **A**ffect is the **A**ction; **E**ffect is the **E**nd result |
| **your / you're** | *your* = belongs to you; *you're* = you are | expand it: does *you are* fit? |
| **who's / whose** | *who's* = who is; *whose* = belongs to whom | expand it |

## The professional pairs
| Pair | Use | Trick |
|---|---|---|
| **principal / principle** | *principal* = main, chief, or a sum of money; *principle* = a rule or belief | the princip**al** is your p**al**; a princip**le** is a ru**le** |
| **complement / compliment** | *complement* = completes or goes well with; *compliment* = praise | compl**e**ment **e**nhances; compl**i**ment: **I** like you |
| **ensure / insure / assure** | *ensure* = make certain; *insure* = buy coverage; *assure* = reassure a person | **in**sure = **in**surance; **as**sure a person |
| **fewer / less** | *fewer* = things you count; *less* = amounts you measure | fewer trucks, less fuel |
| **farther / further** | *farther* = physical distance; *further* = degree, more | **far**ther = **far** on a map |
| **discreet / discrete** | *discreet* = careful, private; *discrete* = separate | in di**scre**te, the *e*'s are **separated** by the *t* |
| **stationary / stationery** | *stationary* = not moving; *stationery* = paper and envelopes | station**e**ry = l**e**tters |
| **adverse / averse** | *adverse* = harmful (*adverse weather*); *averse* = opposed to (*risk-averse*) | **ad**verse = **ad** (bad) conditions |
| **elicit / illicit** | *elicit* = draw out (a response); *illicit* = illegal | **ill**icit = **ill**egal |
| **precede / proceed** | *precede* = come before; *proceed* = go forward | **pre** = before |
| **waive / wave** | *waive* = give up a right (*waive the fee*); *wave* = move your hand | a waiv**er** gives up a right |

sections.md:
## The pairs even editors argue about
- **Disinterested vs uninterested.** *Disinterested* = impartial, with nothing to gain (*a disinterested referee*). *Uninterested* = bored. Many people now use *disinterested* for *bored*, but in formal writing, keep them separate.
- **Comprise vs compose.** The whole **comprises** the parts: *The fleet comprises 12 trucks.* The parts **compose** the whole: *Twelve trucks compose the fleet.* "Comprised of" is very common but still flagged by careful editors; *composed of* or *consists of* is always safe.
- **Fewer vs less with time and money.** *Less than $500* and *less than 10 minutes* are correct, because you're treating the amount as one quantity, not counting dollars or minutes one by one.

sections.title: Fix a real email
sections.problem: "Your going to loose the load if you don't except the rate. Its less trucks then last week."
sections.answer: *"**You're** going to **lose** the load if you don't **accept** the rate. It's **fewer** trucks **than** last week."* Six errors in two sentences, and spell-check catches none of them.

sections.md:
## Loan payments: principal
A loan payment has two parts: **principal** (paying down the amount you borrowed) and **interest** (the lender's fee). Early in a loan, most of each payment is interest. Every extra dollar toward **principal** shrinks the interest you'll pay later. Spelling the word right is good. Understanding it is better.

sections.label: Common traps
sections.md:
- **Alot** isn't a word. It's **a lot** (or *allot*, which means to assign: *allot two hours*).
- **Could care less** literally means you do care a bit. The original is **couldn't care less**.
- **Irregardless** is in dictionaries but marked nonstandard. Use **regardless**.
- **Supposably** → **supposedly**. **For all intensive purposes** → **for all intents and purposes**.

practice.q: "This route is shorter ___ the last one."
"The new tires had a big ___ on fuel mileage."
"The ___ reason I left was the pay."
"Please be ___; this deal isn't public yet."
Fill in: "The broker agreed to ___ the late fee." (give it up)
practice.why: **waive** = give up a right or a charge. A *waiver* is the document.

practice.q: "The jury should be ___: no stake in the outcome."
practice.why: **Disinterested** = impartial. *Uninterested* = bored. A bored jury is a different problem.
practice.hint: Which one means *having nothing to gain*?

practice.q: Which is correct in careful formal writing?
options: The fleet is comprised of 12 trucks.
practice.why: The whole **comprises** the parts, no *of*. *Is composed of* also works.
Not physical distance, but more discussion (degree) → **further**.
practice.hint: Is this about miles on a map?

practice.q: How many errors: "Its alot less work then I thought, irregardless of the weather."
practice.why: **Four**: *Its* → **It's**, *alot* → **a lot**, *then* → **than**, *irregardless* → **regardless**. *Less work* is correct, because work is an amount, not something you count.
practice.hint: Check each word against this lesson. Is *less* right for *work*?
